newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX Alberta gas futures struggle for acceptance.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX Alberta gas futures struggle for acceptance.

text.p: Seven months after their launch, Alberta natural gas futures on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) have not yet broken out of their shell, and many doubt the likelihood of that ever happening.

"There was enough liquidity without it. They were expecting the U.S. to start trading it, but they never showed up. Maybe they need to change it to GJs (C$ per gigajoule) to attract more Canadians," Tony Samaska, a trader at Aquila Canada said.
Like NYMEX's hugely successful Henry Hub, Louisiana, gas futures, the Alberta contract is priced in U.S. dollars per million British thermal units.
The contract specifies delivery at key points along NOVA Gas Transmission, western Canada's main pipeline system.
"If they put it in Canadian dollars per gigajoule, every producer in the city would use it," another Calgary-based trader said, noting the foreign exchange risk was too large for most companies.

"They (NYMEX) thought the big guys who were already trading in U.S. dollars would step up, but they haven't yet. They're looking for some volatility, but it's not there. And with no volatility, there are no floor traders," he added.
Enticing NYMEX to introduce a western Canadian contract was the fact that 10 percent of the gas burned in the U.S. comes from Canada, and 90 percent of that gas is from Alberta.
"We really believe in the contract," a NYMEX spokesperson said, adding the exchange has no plans to change Alberta futures trading to $C/GJ.

But NYMEX is moving to help its floundering contract, saying it is now offering another type of permit that would allow a trader to broker deals for a customer as long as the trader takes responsiblity for two percent of the volume.
NYMEX members are able to purchase this permit, effective the following day, for $5,000, while non-members must apply for a permit, which typically would take six weeks to receive.
"The more liquidity we have available, the better the contract will be," the NYMEX spokesperson said.
The Exchange has said a new contract was needed to monitor the fluctuating natural gas market and sometimes large differentials between the eastern and western markets.
Liquidity in the physical Alberta market at the AECO storage is not a problem, traders said. The hub generally trades in a tight two- to three-cent range on a daily basis.
Most traders argue that a barometer like the Alberta futures contract is not needed.
These negative sentiments are reflected in the contract's recent sessions. No Alberta contracts have traded since March 3 when only five contracts closed.
Open interest for Alberta futures' is only 102 contracts. In its first five days, 652 trades exchanged hands, compared with Henry Hub gas futures' tally of 2,871.
On its first trading day alone, an estimated 2,376 contracts traded for the Kansas City Board of Trade's natgas futures, with a delivery point at Waha in western Texas.
Responding to rumors that KCBT may forge its way into the Canadian futures market, KCBT president Michael Braude said the Board has no plans to introduce a similar contract.
"We have a full-time job with Waha. We're devoting all of our energy to that right now," Braude said.

"We would like to do spread margins with NYMEX. I think we can help each other. We've been doing spread trading with the Chicago Board of Trade for years with wheat, and it's been great," he said, referring to possible spread relationships between either NYMEX's Henry Hub or Permian contract with KCBT's Waha contract.
KCBT's Waha basin-based contract debuted in August 1995, while NYMEX's Permian-based gas contract followed in May 1996.
Permian futures have not traded since January 29, while KCBT's contract this year has averaged more than 300 per day.
